title: Isaac Newton and the South Sea Bubble
text:
In 1720 the South Sea Company took over a large part of the British national debt in exchange for its own shares and promises of trade profits that never really existed. Its share price rose from around 128 pounds in January to about 1,000 pounds by late June, pulling all of London into a frenzy of speculation, then collapsed in the autumn.

Isaac Newton, then Master of the Mint and one of the most admired minds in Europe, held South Sea stock. Records studied by historians, notably the economist Andrew Odlyzko, show that he sold much of it in the spring of 1720 at a large profit. Then, as prices kept soaring and others grew rich, he bought back in during the summer, near the top, at much higher prices. When the bubble burst in the autumn, he lost heavily.

Anecdotes recorded after his death, some of them collected by Joseph Spence, say the loss came to about twenty thousand pounds, a fortune at the time, and attribute to Newton a famous remark: that he could calculate the motions of the heavenly bodies, but not the madness of people. The remark may be embellished, but the pattern of his trades is documented.
lesson: Being right early can tempt you back in when you see others profiting. Intelligence does not protect against crowd psychology, so set your rules before the frenzy, not during it.
source: Andrew Odlyzko (2019). Newton's financial misadventures in the South Sea Bubble. Notes and Records of the Royal Society, 73(1); Joseph Spence, Anecdotes
caveat: The famous quote about the madness of people is first recorded long after Newton's death and may be apocryphal.
